reachable: Yes, and the causality claims are exact — I verified them numerically rather than by reading. On the odd [cmd,obs,...,cmd] layout the instrument builds (L=2r+1, read at 2r, observation withheld), the head's contribution at the read position is live (contrib norm 2.42 against pred norm 16.43 with a non-zero out_proj) and depends on earlier commands and earlier observations. Perturbing obs_i changes the store's contribution at command i by EXACTLY 0.0 and at command i+1 by ~3.0 — the read at step i is taken strictly before step i's write, as claimed, so the withheld observation cannot reach the scored prediction; writing junk into the slot after the read moves the read-position prediction by 6e-7 (fp32 noise). At init the wrapped net is bitwise identical to the unwrapped net (out_proj zero in weight and bias): torch.equal == True. Gradient reaches every head parameter from the genome's real objective (out_proj 65.9, addr_in 10.0, addr_src 1.58, addr_dst 1.17, move_gate 0.045, edit_out 0.50, read_gate 0.066) and the aux alone additionally reaches 127 trunk parameters through the pred-InfoNCE term. All five aux terms are non-zero on a real batch. The optim-interaction claims are exact: addr_src.weight/addr_dst.weight are [64,256] siblings and do route to Muon, out_proj.weight [768,768] does land under the spectral cap, and the cap is a no-op at zero init. Aux compute cost measured at ~3% of step time on CPU (1.862 vs 1.806 s/step), so the author's failure mode 4 is a loss-balance risk, not a speed risk.
solves_outside_model: No — this is clean. Nothing parses a command string anywhere (the batch does not even carry command text); the miner works only on pairwise squared-L2 distances between the batch's own frozen embeddings. Everything mined is used to choose WHICH training positions get a loss and what that loss's endpoint is, which is the permitted category. The aux is train-time only — aux_loss is called nowhere but evolve/harness.py:_train, and it needs the observation at the answer position, which is the ordinary training target and is present at every training position. At scoring time the only thing the head adds to the forward path is sigmoid(read_gate(cmd_feat_i)) * out_proj(read_i), and I confirmed by execution that read_i is a function of the command embeddings up to i and the observations strictly before i. No resolved routing reaches the model's input at the read position; the prior-retraction shape (stamping a Python-resolved answer into the read token) is absent, and this head touches no tokens at all.
summary: The mechanism is real and is implemented as described. The crossover provenance checks out (r23's dual unit source/destination addresses + delta-rule store from the parent; r18's FiLM edit s*(1+tanh(gamma)*gscale)+beta from the partner, both reproduced faithfully in an arch-independent head), the addressing supervision genuinely is something neither parent computes, the store is causal at the scored position to floating-point exactness, the net is bitwise unchanged at init, and every claim about the optimizer interaction (Muon on the [64,256] address sibling pair, spectral cap on the [768,768] readout, no-op at zero) is literally true. The mining rule works far better on real data than the author could have known: it separates mutating from contentful steps perfectly on 64 real rows with a wide cluster-size margin, and 1183 of 1219 mined cat->cat pairs are genuine routed reads whose content really does land at the path being read. The one substantive gap between the hypothesis and reality is purity of the mined set: the rule also admits `ls -1 /` -> `ls -a` pairs with no routing at all, and because the example weight is the count of intervening mutations, those row-spanning pairs get the largest weights — 27% of the aux gradient weight supervises an address chain that does not exist, against 29% on the depth-3/4 slice the objective is actually about. Two smaller claims are overstated: "deeper routings dominate" (the weight is intervening-mutation count, not this content's hop count) and "the degenerate solution is structurally penalised" (the counterweight is ~37x weaker per position than the term pushing the other way; measured at 0.012 of an 8.60 aux total). The quoted jail-row numbers (26 steps / 8 mutating) do not match the file cited (31 steps / 9), though the conclusion drawn from them holds with a bigger margin. Separately worth recording for interpreting the result: the parent's head was structurally disabled under the parent's own arch, so this is an add-a-mechanism delta, not a swap, and the aux at full ramp is ~3x the genome's objective (address CE alone is 66% of it) — this candidate re-weights training rather than adding a side term.

divergences.claim: "Everything my aux uses is mined from the batch's own embeddings by these two tests" + "A routed read is a step whose observation duplicates an EARLIER step's observation while its COMMAND differs, with at least one mutating step in between ... is exactly that pattern." The hypothesis presents the mined set as being routed reads.
divergences.what_the_code_does: The rule is implemented exactly as stated, and on real data it is mostly right: 1183 of 1219 mined `cat`->`cat` pairs are genuine routed reads (I followed the actual file chain in the trajectory JSON and the exposed content really does land at the path read at j). But the rule also admits pairs that involve no routing at all — `ls -1 /` -> `ls -a` / `ls`, whose directory listings are near-duplicates under the 5%-of-mean-distance test while the commands differ. Because the per-example weight is n_mut and those pairs straddle the entire row, they receive the LARGEST weights and survive the top-k cap. Measured over 8 real 64-row batches: 27.3% of the total aux example weight goes to non-routed `ls` pairs and a further 2.2% to pairs whose chain is broken. For that ~30% the address-chase recurrence supervises a chain that does not exist, i.e. it teaches the move-command gates to open on an address that no move touched.

divergences.claim: "Examples are weighted by the number of mutating steps between i and j, so deeper routings dominate the gradient" — offered as the reason the aux targets the eligible depth-3/4 slice.
divergences.what_the_code_does: `wt = n_mut` counts every mutating step between i and j, of any content, not the number of hops this content took. The correlation is real but loose: n_mut=1 -> mean true hops 1.00, n_mut=4 -> 1.66, n_mut=9 -> 3.89. Weight actually landing on true depth 3-4 (the eligible slice) is 28.8%; true depth 1 gets 25.1%; non-routed pairs get the single largest share at 27.3%. "Deeper routings dominate" is directionally true and quantitatively false.

divergences.claim: "The degenerate solution is structurally penalised, not just discouraged ... under the lazy solution the logits at i and at j are equal and the loss floors at log 2. Beating that floor requires f to actually move away from a_dst[i], and the only parameterised route for f to move is through g_t."
divergences.what_the_code_does: The log-2 arithmetic is right, but there is a second parameterised route out of the floor that the hypothesis does not acknowledge: lower <a_src[i], a_dst[i]> so position i's logit drops and the lazy a_src[j]~=a_dst[i] solution wins outright with the gates shut. The only thing opposing that is self_addr_weight, and its per-position coefficient is 0.1 / N_contentful (~1400 live contentful steps in a 64-row batch) ~= 7e-5, against 0.5 * w_e ~= 2.6e-3 for the address CE at a mined example — roughly 37x weaker. Measured on a real batch at full ramp the self-agreement term contributes 0.012 out of an 8.60 aux total. The mechanism is discouraged, not structurally penalised. (A stronger argument the author did not make does hold: a_src/a_dst are one shared map over command embeddings, so dst(cat P) = src(cat Q) cannot be satisfied globally for the arbitrary P->Q pairings that appear across rows.)
